text: The men digging the canal were paid every other Saturday, at the alehouse by the lock. The contractor's agent had an arrangement with the landlord, and part of each man's wages came as tickets that no other house would take. A fair share of a fortnight's work was spent in the room where it was paid.
strengths: gives the rule behind the scene instead of the scene itself
the arrangement between agent and landlord is explained in one plain sentence
the last line lands the consequence without calling it unfair
weaknesses: needs a picture of the pay table or the alehouse to sit over
the share spent at the bar is left vague, so a film that has the figure should use it
spokenRhythm: A medium line sets the day and place, a longer one explains the arrangement, and a shorter one closes on the consequence.
narrativeFunction: Turns an ordinary payday into the arrangement that sent much of the men's pay straight back over the landlord's counter.
whyItWorks: The picture can show men queuing at a table, but only the narration can say who arranged it and where the money went. The dry closing sentence trusts the listener to see the trap without being told it was one.

text: The keeper's log for that night has the lamp lit at ten past five. The service required an entry every four hours, and a keeper who missed one could be dismissed. The next entry is at dawn, and it is signed by his assistant.
strengths: the rule is given before the gap, so the listener measures the gap
the reveal is a signature on the page, not a hint
the record is kept in the present tense and the rule in the past, so source and history stay distinct
weaknesses: depends on the film going on to say where the keeper was
leaves the listener to count the missing entries, which some will not do
spokenRhythm: Three steady sentences, the middle one longest, the last one settling on the name at the foot of the entry.
narrativeFunction: Opens a question inside a quiet archive scene by setting the rule and then showing the record breaking it.
whyItWorks: A shot of an old logbook shows ink and paper. The narration supplies the time, the regulation and the penalty, so the missing hours carry weight before anyone calls them strange. The assistant's signature is stated as a fact of the document and never dramatised.

text: A claim on the creek ran fifty feet along the water. Under the camp's own rules, a man kept his claim only as long as he worked it, and ground left idle for ten days could be staked by anyone who came along. So a good deal of the digging that summer was done for the benefit of whoever was watching.
strengths: each number arrives in its own sentence with its own job
the camp's rule explains the busyness on screen
the dry closing observation grows out of the rule rather than being added to it
weaknesses: the middle sentence carries the rule and its penalty together and is the longest breath in the passage
the closing line would lose its effect if the film leaned on this kind of joke often
spokenRhythm: A short factual opener, a long rule that runs to its penalty, then a medium line that turns the rule into a smile.
narrativeFunction: Explains why a crowded creek bank looked busier than it was.
whyItWorks: Footage or engravings of men at work show effort. The narration gives the rule that produced the effort and lets the listener draw the wry conclusion. The size of the claim and the ten days are both things a listener can hold.

text: The mill bell rang at half past five, and the gate was shut when it stopped. Anyone who came after that lost a quarter of a day's pay. The clock that decided it hung in the owner's office, and the spinners always said it ran fast. Nobody else in the street owned a clock that could settle the matter.
strengths: the penalty is measured in pay the workers would feel
the complaint is reported as what the spinners said, not as fact
the last line explains why the complaint could never be tested
weaknesses: four sentences of similar weight, so it relies on the reading to vary the pace
spokenRhythm: Even sentences that tighten from the bell to the penalty, then ease into the dry final observation.
narrativeFunction: Sets the rule of the working day and the workers' grievance about it in one beat.
whyItWorks: The picture can show a gate and a bell. Only the narration can say what lateness cost and who owned the time. The claim that the clock ran fast stays a claim, and the reason it stays one is itself the point.

text: The telegraph company charged by the word. So the merchants who used it most wrote in code. One word in their code books might stand for a whole sentence about the price of cotton. The clerks sent thousands of these words a day, and had no idea what any of them meant.
strengths: the tariff comes first, so the code arrives as a consequence rather than a curiosity
one word standing for a sentence makes the saving easy to grasp by ear
the clerks' ignorance is stated plainly and left to be funny on its own
weaknesses: the closing observation is a familiar wry shape and should not sit next to another one in the same sequence
spokenRhythm: Two short sentences of cause and response, a longer one for the mechanism, and a long close that ends on the clerks.
narrativeFunction: Explains why the message forms on screen look like nonsense, and who could and could not read them.
whyItWorks: The picture shows clerks at their keys and forms covered in strange words. The narration supplies the price that made the code worth inventing, and the fact that the men sending it could not read it, which no image can show.

text: Nobody in the room insured the ship alone. Each man who signed the slip took a share of the risk and wrote the sum beside his name. If she came home, they divided the premium between them. If she was lost, each of them owed what he had written, and not a shilling more.
strengths: explains shared underwriting with plain verbs like signed, divided and owed
the two outcomes are given side by side so the listener can weigh them
the closing phrase makes the limit of each man's risk concrete
weaknesses: premium is left unexplained and relies on the film having used the word earlier
the paired if sentences should not be repeated elsewhere in the same section
spokenRhythm: A short opening statement, a longer explanation, then two balanced conditionals with the second one running a little longer.
narrativeFunction: Turns a crowded room of men signing a paper into an explanation of how shared underwriting worked.
whyItWorks: The picture shows a paper being passed and signed. The narration explains what each signature committed a man to, and in what circumstances, so the scene becomes a lesson in risk without sounding like one.
